name: Peltzman Effect
description: When a product, policy, or environment feels safer, people may respond by taking more risk elsewhere, offsetting some of the intended safety gain. The extra protection gets spent behaviorally instead of being preserved fully.
design_relevance_note: Relevant to guardrails, fraud controls, warnings, moderation systems, privacy/security affordances, and automation features: adding protection can change behavior, sometimes encouraging bolder or less careful action rather than simply reducing harm.
myth_risk_note: Hedlund (2000) confirms risk compensation is a real phenomenon in some safety contexts, consistent with the entry's existing partial status. But the HIV-prevention literature -- the largest and most contemporary test case found in this pass -- consistently finds NO behavioral risk compensation: the PROUD trial (McCormack et al. 2015) found no STI difference despite a hint of risk compensation in some recipients; Fonner et al.'s (2016) meta-analysis of oral PrEP found 'no evidence of behavioral risk compensation'; and O Murchu et al.'s (2022) comprehensive meta-analysis found no evidence for increased sexual risk behavior or STIs with PrEP use. The Peltzman effect appears highly context-dependent rather than a universal design law, and its most rigorously tested modern domain finds it largely absent.
prevalence_note: Named mostly in safety, trust-and-safety, security, transport, and public-health-adjacent design conversations rather than in mainstream baseline UX heuristics lists.

findings.description: A systematic review and meta-analysis of 18 studies on oral HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) found PrEP significantly reduces HIV acquisition risk, with consistently NO association found between PrEP use and changes in sexual risk behavior -- a rigorous, large-scale null result for behavioral risk compensation in a domain where it was theoretically plausible (a safety intervention against a serious risk). Real evidence supporting this entry's own existing 'context-dependent, not universal' characterization: risk compensation is a real phenomenon in some safety contexts but is genuinely absent in this well-studied modern one.
findings.effect_size: risk ratio = 0.30, 95% CI [0.21, 0.45] for PrEP effectiveness with >70% adherence; no significant association found between PrEP use and sexual risk behavior change
findings.source_title: Effectiveness and safety of oral HIV preexposure prophylaxis for all populations

findings.description: Reviewing safety-regulation and injury-prevention evidence, Hedlund concludes that risk compensation is a real possibility but not a universal constant: added safety can sometimes be offset by riskier behavior, yet the size and even presence of the effect vary substantially by context and are often overstated in simple popular retellings.
findings.source_title: Risky business: safety regulations, risk compensation, and individual behavior
